## A deliberately modest promise

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}

Write one model in a restricted, Julia-flavoured language:

```julia
model = @slic (; x, y) begin
    alpha ~ normal(0, 2)
    beta  ~ normal(0, 1)
    sigma ~ exponential(1)
    y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma)
end
```

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="42%"}

Get ordinary, inspectable Stan:

```stan
parameters {
  real alpha;
  real beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma ~ exponential(1);
  y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x,
             sigma);
}
```

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
StanBlocks is a frontend, not a replacement for Stan.
:::

<p class="small muted fragment">… with quality-of-life improvements such as activity analysis, submodels, user-defined types (currently enabling e.g. NamedTuples and ragged data structures), higher-order user-defined functions, closures, keyword &amp; default arguments, automatic but optional type &amp; shape inference, (ragged) plates, metaprogramming, Julia-style multiple dispatch, and more.</p>

::: {.notes}
Open with the boundary, not the feature list. The promise is deliberately
small: author in Julia syntax, emit normal Stan, keep Stan's toolchain.
:::

# 1. Why? {.section-slide}

Why put a language in front of an already good language?

## Julia + performant AD versus Stan

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Julia + performant AD

- expressive, general-purpose language
- mathematical code may need expert rewriting
- AD must cope with that full expressiveness
- historically incomplete, wrong, or slow
- Enzyme makes far more possible today

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="48%"}

### Stan

- restricted language for statistical models
- obvious mathematical code is a strong baseline
- AD is central to the inference stack
- narrower target is easier to optimize reliably
- generated code remains inspectable

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Julia maximizes **expressive freedom**; Stan narrows the problem to make differentiable programs **predictable**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The first Julia bullet pair folds in Michael Tiemann's framing from
[“Julia Solves the 2 Language Problem, However It Creates the 1.5 Language
Problem”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RUJFd-rEa0k): naive Julia can look
like the mathematics yet be much slower than expert Julia, whose performant
implementation may look very different. The detailed causes are not the point
of this slide. The AD comparison is our synthesis, not Tiemann's framing.
Historically, Julia AD has often felt incomplete, incorrect, or insufficiently
performant. Julia did not bake one performant AD path into Core, while the
language's generality already gives the primal compiler a difficult
optimization problem. Differentiating the full language makes the analysis
harder still. Stan accepts the opposite constraint: its narrower language and
runtime are designed around differentiation for statistical inference.

Enzyme changes what is possible in principle and can already match or beat Stan
on some workloads. Do not turn that into “every Julia program always works
today”: compilation, activity analysis, custom rules, library coverage, and
workload-specific performance still matter. In StanBlocks today, Mooncake is
the Julia AD backend; Stan's path is separate and uses Stan Math through
BridgeStan.
:::

## The Stan bargain

:::: {.card-grid}
::: {.card}

<div class="card-title">“Not ideal, but good” performance</div>

Out of the box. Not always the theoretical optimum—but mature vectorisation,
fused kernels, reverse-mode AD, and NUTS adaptation make “write the obvious
model” a strong baseline.

:::
::: {.card .blue-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Reliability</div>

Static checks, explicit constraints and Jacobians, a mature sampler, and years
of use on difficult models.

:::
::: {.card .gold-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Stable semantics</div>

The generated target is a small, explicit language designed around Bayesian
computation rather than general-purpose execution.

:::
::: {.card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">A review boundary</div>

`stan_code(model)` is the boundary between a compositional authoring language
and a mature inference language — read it, diff it, archive it, check it with
`stanc`, hand it to the Stan ecosystem.

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
“Generated” does not have to mean “opaque.”
:::

::: {.notes}
Use the user's wording verbally: “not ideal, but good performance out of the
box.” The point is engineering leverage, not a benchmark claim that Stan wins
every workload.
:::

# 2. What? {.section-slide}

A small declarative model surface with a surprisingly high ceiling.

## One model declaration

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### StanBlocks source

```julia
m = @slic (; x, y) begin
    alpha ~ normal(0, 2)
    beta  ~ normal(0, 1)
    sigma ~ exponential(1)

    mu = alpha + beta * x
    y ~ normal(mu, sigma)
end
```

What is missing?

- block declarations
- types and shapes

*Main caveat* — model-level control flow: keep `@slic` flat; use `@deffun` or `plate`.

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="49%"}

### Essential Stan emission

```stan
data {
  int x_n; vector[x_n] x;
  int y_n; vector[y_n] y;
}
parameters {
  real alpha; real beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[x_n] mu = alpha + beta * x;
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2);
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma ~ exponential(1);
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[y_n] y_likelihood = ...;
  vector[y_n] y_gen = ...;
}
```

:::
::::

:::: {.card-grid .three .compact-cards}
::: {.card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Placement</div>

`data` · `transformed data` · `parameters` · `transformed parameters` · `model` · `generated quantities`

:::
::: {.card .blue-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Representation</div>

types · shapes · constraints · function signatures · captured dimensions

:::
::: {.card .gold-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Workflow outputs</div>

pointwise log likelihood · posterior predictive draws · executable model descriptor

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This output was generated from the current checkout. “Essential” means helper
functions in the functions block are omitted on this slide; the backup has the
full relevant declarations. The three cards are what the compiler INFERS from
the one declaration: block placement; representation (types, shapes,
constraints, function signatures, captured dimensions); and workflow outputs
(pointwise log-likelihood, posterior-predictive draws, the executable
descriptor). The one real restriction is model-level control flow — @slic
bodies are straight-line; loops and branches live in @deffun or plate.
:::

## Composition is the reason for the frontend

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}

### Reusable submodel

```julia
@slic random_slope(x::vector[n]) = begin
    beta ~ normal(0, 1)
    return beta * x
end

m = @slic (; x, y) begin
    eta ~ random_slope(x)
    y ~ normal(eta, 1)
end
```

Emits a prefixed parameter `eta_beta`.

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="47%"}

### Post-hoc variant

```julia
wide_prior = Base.merge(random_slope, quote
    beta ~ normal(0, 5)
end)
```

The matching `beta` statement is replaced; `random_slope` stays unchanged.

The same mechanism supports:

- nested submodels
- swapping in new data
- typed positional arguments
- generated model variants

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The payoff grows with a *family* of bespoke models, not with the first ten-line model.
:::

# 3. How? {.section-slide}

Julia syntax on the front, SlicStan's information-flow idea in the middle, Stan on the back.

## The intellectual lineage: SlicStan

StanBlocks is directly inspired by [Gorinova, Gordon & Sutton (POPL 2019)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3290348). Shared ideas: no author-written Stan blocks, placement inferred from information flow, composable model fragments, and Stan preserved as the inference target.

::: {.fragment}
| | SlicStan | StanBlocks.jl (MlicStan?) |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | A new Stan-like language | A restricted Julia macro DSL |
| Core analysis | Information-flow type system | Forward trace + reverse likelihood tracking |
| Abstraction | Flexible model functions | Julia dispatch, closures, kwargs, macros, `@slic` submodels |
| Distinctive reach | Formal semantics; marginalizing out discrete parameters | Auto generated quantities, model variants, descriptors, BridgeStan/Julia integration |
| Implementation posture | Research implementation in F# | Julia package used by larger Julia model DSLs |
| Output | Stan | Stan |
:::

::: {.notes}
Credit Maria Gorinova explicitly. SlicStan is “Slightly Less Intensely
Constrained Stan.” Its paper gives an operational density semantics and a
semantics-preserving translation; StanBlocks does not claim that formal result.
:::

## One model, three activity analyses

```julia
m = @slic (; y, subject) begin
    J     = maximum(subject)
    mu    ~ normal(0, 1)
    tau   ~ exponential(1)
    alpha :: vector[J] ~ normal(mu, tau)   # per-subject effect
    sigma ~ exponential(1)
    y ~ normal(alpha[subject], sigma)
end
```

Same source. Only the **data you bind** changes — activity analysis and metadata
decide, per statement, where each sampling statement ends up.

:::: {.card-grid .three}
::: {.card .gold-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Prior prediction</div>

Bind **no outcome** — `m(; subject)`.

Nothing to condition on, so the whole model forward-simulates in `generated
quantities` — `mu, tau, alpha, sigma`, and `y` itself.

:::
::: {.card .blue-card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Posterior fit</div>

Bind **`y` observed**.

`y ~ normal(alpha[subject], sigma)` becomes the likelihood; `mu, tau, alpha,
sigma` are fitted, and `y_gen` is the posterior-predictive replica.

:::
::: {.card .fragment}

<div class="card-title">Population prediction · CV</div>

Bind **`maybecv(:subject, subject)`**.

Taint flows from the grouping into `alpha`: the per-subject effects leave
`parameters` and re-draw from `normal(mu, tau)` in `generated quantities`,
while `mu, tau, sigma` stay fitted.

:::
::::

```{=html}
<p class="stan-modal-cta fragment">
<button type="button" class="stan-modal-trigger"
  onclick="event.stopPropagation(); window.openStanModal('prior-posterior');">
  See the generated Stan, side by side&nbsp;→
</button>
</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The SAME @slic source is all three models; only the data binding differs, and
two mechanisms do the work. (1) Dead-parameter elimination: bind y and `y ~`
is a live likelihood, so mu, tau, alpha, sigma are fitted parameters; OMIT y
and there is no likelihood at all, so the whole model forward-simulates in
generated quantities (y is generated too — this is the prior predictive). (2)
cv taint: maybecv on the subject index taints everything it reaches — the y
likelihood (dropped) and, because alpha's size J = maximum(subject) is tainted,
alpha itself, which relocates to generated quantities and re-draws from
normal(mu, tau). mu, tau, sigma are untainted, so they stay parameters. That is
leave-a-group-out / population prediction. The typed `alpha :: vector[J] ~
normal(mu, tau)` and the `; n=J` spelling now emit byte-identical Stan under cv
taint — the declared size carries the taint too (StanBlocks fix, snag
`typed-lhs-size-c-8a7fbfb2`). The modal shows the real distilled `stan_code`.
:::

# 4. Started pre-agents — still relevant? {.section-slide}

Yes, but the value proposition changes.

## From keystroke savings to a model contract

<div class="timeline">
  <div><strong>Oct 2024</strong>Initial repository: block inference, Julia syntax, Stan emission.</div>
  <div><strong>2025</strong>Production-shaped models, generated quantities, broader Stan surface.</div>
  <div><strong>2026</strong>Agent-assisted expansion: <code>plate</code>s, closures, higher-order functions, hardening.</div>
</div>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment width="47%"}

### Agents make this cheaper

- write Stan boilerplate
- translate a sketch into a full model
- generate repetitive signatures and tests
- explore compiler edge cases quickly
- producing, finding, and fixing bugs

:::
::: {.column .fragment width="49%"}

### Agents do not make this disappear

- one source for a family of model variants
- a reusable statistical vocabulary
- generated Stan that humans and tools can inspect

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Agents reduce the cost of writing code. StanBlocks reduces the amount of *independent model meaning* we have to maintain.
:::

::: {.notes}
Avoid claiming that generated code is automatically correct. The point is that
the compiler centralises repeated semantics and exposes the result for review.
Agents have also been valuable adversarial testers; they make the language more
feasible to build while raising expectations for its contracts.
:::

# 5. What next? {.section-slide}

Move up a layer without hiding the layer below.

## StanBlocks as *one* compiler layer

<div class="flow">
  <div class="step j-blue"><strong>BRM.jl</strong><br>formulae, terms, priors, model-family vocabulary</div>
  <div class="step stan"><strong>StanBlocks.jl</strong><br>composition, tracing, block/type/shape inference</div>
  <div class="step j-green"><strong>BridgeStan.jl</strong><br>compiled Stan model — log density &amp; gradients (AD)</div>
  <div class="step j-purple"><strong>JuliaBayes.jl</strong><br>shared Julia-facing workflow and ecosystem integration</div>
</div>

::: {.fragment}
The largest current public (but unregistered) consumer is [BayesianRegressionModels.jl](https://github.com/nsiccha/BayesianRegressionModels.jl): a `brms`-like formula layer that _currently_ lowers into Stan via StanBlocks.jl, but will target Julia via Turing.jl as well in the future.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Near-term priorities:

1. Make BRM.jl the ergonomic route for standard regression families.
2. Keep StanBlocks available for bespoke PKPD and other compositional models.
3. Connect through JuliaBayes interfaces rather than inventing another closed workflow.
:::

## Summary {.summary-slide}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}

### The pitch

1. **Julia + AD maximizes expressiveness; Stan narrows the problem** to make differentiable statistical programs predictable.
2. **Stan is a strong inference target**: reliable, good out of the box, and explicit.
3. **StanBlocks makes model families composable** while keeping generated Stan inspectable.
4. **Agents strengthen the case for a compiler contract**, even as they weaken the case for mere syntax reduction.

# Backup {.section-slide}

Source-to-emission examples and the honest edges of the current language.

## Backup · deterministic control flow belongs in `@deffun`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}

```julia
@deffun centered_sum(x) = begin
    xbar = mean(x)
    acc = 0.0
    for xi in x
        acc += xi - xbar
    end
    acc
end
```

:::
::: {.column width="47%"}

```stan
real centered_sum(vector x) {
  real xbar = mean(x);
  real acc = 0.0;
  for (i in 1:num_elements(x)) {
    real xi = x[i];
    acc += xi - xbar;
  }
  return acc;
}
```

:::
::::

`@slic` stays flat; `@deffun` owns loops, branches, mutation, iteration, and bounded comprehensions.

## Backup · higher-order functions specialize at compile time

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}

```julia
@deffun apply_twice(f, x) = f(f(x))

# f is passed like data — pick any callee
z = apply_twice(exp, mu)   # ⇒ exp(exp(mu))
```

:::
::: {.column width="47%"}

```stan
real apply_twice_exp(real x) {
  return exp(exp(x));
}

// at the call site:
real z = apply_twice_exp(mu);
```

:::
::::

The function argument is resolved at compile time: StanBlocks emits one specialized Stan function per callee (`apply_twice_exp`), so no runtime function object ever reaches Stan.

## Backup · `plate` is the loop that samples

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}

```julia
theta ~ plate(y; outer = 4) do yi
    t ~ normal(mu0, 1)
    yi ~ normal(t, sigma)
    t
end
```

:::
::: {.column width="47%"}

```stan
parameters {
  vector[4] theta_t;
}
transformed parameters {
  for (i in 1:4)
    theta[i] = theta_t[i];
}
model {
  for (i in 1:4) {
    theta_t[i] ~ normal(mu0, 1);
    y[i] ~ normal(theta_t[i], sigma);
  }
}
```

:::
::::

`plate` promotes fresh cell variables to outer storage and clones the compiler-owned loop into the Stan blocks that need it.

## Backup · missing continuous outcomes

```julia
m = @slic (; y = Union{Missing,Float64}[1.0, missing, 3.0]) begin
    mu ~ normal(0, 2)
    sigma ~ exponential(1)
    y ~ normal(mu, sigma)
end
```

Essential rewrite:

```stan
data { vector[y_obs_n] y_obs; array[...] int y_ii_obs; array[...] int y_ii_mis; }
parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
model { y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma); }
generated quantities {
  vector[y_ii_mis_n] y_mis = normal_vector_rng(y_ii_mis_n, mu, sigma);
  vector[...] y = merge_missing(y_obs, y_mis, y_ii_obs, y_ii_mis);
}
```

The usual case adds no missing-value sampler dimensions: imputed values are posterior-predictive generated quantities.

## Backup · observation semantics compose with a base family

```julia
y_weighted  ~ weighted(normal, w, mu, sigma)
y_truncated ~ truncated(normal, mu, sigma; lower=lo, upper=hi)
y_censored  ~ censored(normal, mu, sigma; lower=lo, upper=hi)
y_interval  ~ interval_censored(normal, lo, hi, mu, sigma)
```

The compiler selects the matching:

- aggregate density/mass function
- pointwise companion
- CDF/CCDF terms
- predictive RNG

For censoring, the emitted density uses tail mass at the threshold atoms and the predictive RNG clamps a base-family draw.

## Backup · executable descriptor

For the regression example:

```text
inputs:
  y      observed=true
  x      observed=false

outputs:
  alpha, beta, sigma   parameter / posterior
  y_likelihood        generated_quantity / pointwise_loglik / source=y
  y_gen               generated_quantity / draw / source=y

operations:
  transpile · instantiate · fit · predict · pointwise_loglik
```

Consumers do not need a parallel registry of what a model can do.

## Backup · current hard edges

| Boundary | Current rule |
|---|---|
| Model-level control flow | Keep `@slic` flat; use `@deffun` or `plate` |
| `plate` recursion / scan | Cells must be independent; use a deterministic recurrence |
| Plate cell shape | Scalars and fixed vectors; no matrix-valued cell result |
| General containers | No general 3-D+ Julia container surface |
| Missing data | Continuous outcomes only; no missing predictors or discrete parameters |
| Ragged observations | Continuous; groupwise log likelihood; no ragged integer draws |
| Arbitrary Julia calls | Register through `@deffun`/builtins; no opaque auto-transpilation |
| Validation | `transpiles` is not enough: run `stanc` and semantic/gradient checks |

::: {.takeaway}
A small language is useful only when its “no” is explicit.
:::
